'''Aleksandr Leonidovich Khazanov''' (May 4, 1979 – disappeared June 10, 2001) is a [[Russian American]] [[mathematician]]. A [[child prodigy]], he wrote a perfect paper at the [[International Mathematical Olympiad]] 1994,<ref>{{Cite web | title = Perfect Score for Americans in World Math Tourney | url = https://www.nytimes.com/1994/07/20/us/perfect-score-for-americans-in-world-math-tourney.html | first = Sam |last = Dillon| website = [[The New York Times]] | date = July 20, 1994 | access-date = December 27, 2014 }}</ref>  [[List of International Mathematical Olympiad participants#Exceptionally young medalists|one of the youngest ever to do so]]. Khazanov was reported missing in June 2001.<ref name="nydailynews">{{cite news |url=http://www.nydailynews.com/archives/news/b-klyn-student-22-missing-week-article-1.900654|title=B'klyn Student, 22, Missing A Week |first=Martin |last=Mbugua |newspaper=[[New York Daily News]] |date=June 17, 2001 }}</ref> He suffered from depression or bipolar disorder at the time of his disappearance.

==Biography==
Born to Anna and Leonid Khazanov, a math professor, Aleksandr had attended a special school for math students several years older in [[Leningrad]], [[Soviet Union]] (now [[Saint Petersburg, Russia]]), before his family fled [[Antisemitism|antisemitic]] threats and moved to [[Brooklyn, New York]], United States as refugees in 1992. He attended [[Stuyvesant High School]] and showed his exceptional talent in mathematics. In the summer of 1994, he passed qualifying exams for [[Penn State University]]'s doctoral program in math, and he was the youngest member on the United States team for the [[International Mathematical Olympiad]] of which all six members received perfect scores. In the following year, he was named a finalist and eventually placed 7th at the 54th [[Westinghouse Science Talent Search]] for a paper dealing with a variant of [[Fermat's Last Theorem]], mentored by [[Leonid Vaserstein]], a math professor at Penn State University, and also from Russia.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Khazanov |first=Alex |year=1995 |title=Fermat's Equation in Matrices |journal=Serdica Mathematical Journal |volume=21 |issue=1 |pages=19–40 |url=http://www.math.bas.bg/serdica/1995/1995-019-040.pdf }}</ref><ref name="nytimes">{{Cite news |title=At 15, Westinghouse Finalist Grasps 'Holy Grail' of Math |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |date=January 25, 1995 |first=Pam |last=Belluck |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1995/01/25/nyregion/at-15-westinghouse-finalist-grasps-holy-grail-of-math.html }}</ref> He represented the United States for the second time in the 1995 International Mathematical Olympiad, and he entered the PhD math program at [[Penn State University]] right after high school in fall 1995.<ref name="nypost">{{cite news|url=https://nypost.com/2001/06/17/genius-immigrant-missing-in-bklyn/|title=Genius immigrant missing in B'klyn|first= Philip |last= Messing|work=New York Post|date=June 17, 2001|access-date=June 18, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.the-scientist.com/notebook-old/notebook-58495|title=Notebook|work=The Scientist Magazine|date=June 12, 1995|volume=9|number=12|page=30|access-date=June 18, 2019}}</ref>

==Disappearance==
In the morning of June 10, 2001, he left home with his mountain bike and went missing, leaving a note in Russian saying "I went to a library." He was taking a semester leave due to personal problems, and had been taking drugs for depression, but he did not bring them when he left home.<ref name="nypost" /><ref name="nydailynews" />
